name: Pre-Tamanic
region: Upper Kapuas, Kapuas Hulu Regency, West Kalimantan
notes: The common ancestor of the Tamanic dialects, which Adelaar does not reconstruct as such: Table 1 (p. 5) gives one 'Tamanic' column of changes from PMP, and the dialects 'are mutually intelligible' (p. 33). Entered as an earlier stage of Tamanic with that column (decision adelaar1994a-tamanic). Adelaar puts Tamanic with the South Sulawesi languages, most significantly on PMP *j (Tamanic s, PSS *z), *Z (Tamanic d-, -r-, PSS *d, *r) and the retention of *w- (p. 32), and is 'inclined' to subgroup it with Buginese (Figure 3, pp. 34-35); listed here as a proposed daughter of PSS. Blust (1981) and Nothofer (1988) had put Embaloh in Malayic; Hudson (1970) first in Malayic-Dayak, later (1978) as an 'exo-Bornean' group with affinities to Buginese (pp. 2-4). Tamanic keeps PMP final consonants in final position, which no borrowing from South Sulawesi could explain (p. 33).
inherit_note: PMP phonemes that Table 1 and §3.1 do not discuss are carried down unchanged.

name: Embaloh
region: Embaloh, Leboyan, Lauh, Palin, Nyabau and Mandai tributaries of the upper Kapuas
notes: Adelaar's main Tamanic data, from his field work in Benua Martinus (1989); 'a more conservative phonology than the other Tamanic dialects' (p. 1). 'Maloh' is an Iban exonym; the speakers call themselves Embaloh or Ambalo (p. 1 n. 1). Tamanic developments shown by the examples (pp. 6-7): vowel contraction (*-aya, *aCa with a lost laryngeal > aː: ba-raː 'big', daːn 'branch'), sporadic dissimilation of u to i before u (timpul < *tumpul), l > r before a following r (urar < *ulaR, intaror < *qatəluR), and an unexplained final glottal stop, an areal feature of Borneo.
